pi.name: Morgan DeSantis
pi.title: Assistant Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: Morgan DeSantis is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology at the University of Michigan. She earned her Ph.D. from the University of Pennsylvania. Her lab investigates how microtubule-associated motor proteins, especially cytoplasmic dynein, transport cellular cargo, how motor activity is regulated, and how motor dysfunction relates to neurodevelopmental disease, using single-molecule TIRF microscopy, live-cell fluorescence microscopy, protein biochemistry, and cryo-electron microscopy.

description: The DeSantis lab studies microtubule-associated motor proteins, which transport cellular cargo including organelles, mRNA, viruses, and protein aggregates. The lab focuses on cytoplasmic dynein, a 1.5 MDa motor complex that moves cargo toward the cell interior. Researchers ask how dynein is assembled in living cells, how binding proteins such as Lis1, Ndel1, and cargo adaptors modify its activity, how it binds and transports specific cargoes, how it is correctly localized within cells, and how its dysfunction contributes to disease. The group combines single-molecule TIRF microscopy, protein biochemistry, cryo-electron microscopy, and live-cell imaging.

areas.title: Dynein motor assembly and activation
areas.summary: The lab investigates how the 1.5 MDa dynein complex is assembled in living cells and how regulators such as Lis1, Ndel1, and cargo adaptors control the mechanism and kinetics of dynein activation.

areas.title: Cargo recognition and transport
areas.summary: Researchers study how dynein binds and transports specific cargoes, including organelles, mRNA, viruses (e.g., HIV-1), and protein aggregates, and how adaptor identity dictates transport.

areas.title: Dynein localization and disease
areas.summary: The group examines how dynein is properly localized within cells (e.g., gating at the cell periphery by CCSer2) and how impaired motor function is associated with neurodevelopmental and other diseases.
